stemMd: Suppose the class repeated the study with every tray propped at $5^{\circ}$, changing nothing else. Based on Table 5, the runoff from the bare-soil tray would most likely have been closest to:
explanationMd:
Start with the direction of the effect, because it settles the question before any arithmetic. For every cover in Table 5, raising the slope from $10^{\circ}$ to $20^{\circ}$ *increased* runoff. Lowering the slope below $10^{\circ}$ should therefore *decrease* it, so the prediction must be **less than the $10^{\circ}$ bare-soil value of $1120$ mL**. Only $940$ mL is below $1120$ mL; the other three choices ($1180$, $1300$ and $1520$ mL) are all above it and all describe runoff rising as the ground is made flatter.

Now check that $940$ mL is a reasonable size. Over the $10^{\circ}$ the slope was raised, bare-soil runoff rose by $1480 - 1120 = 360$ mL, which is

$$\frac{360\text{ mL}}{10^{\circ}} = 36\ \text{mL per degree}.$$

Going $5^{\circ}$ the other way from $10^{\circ}$ should subtract about $5 \times 36 = 180$ mL, giving $1120 - 180 = 940$ mL.

Check the reasoning against the physical picture in the passage: water that does not run off soaks in. A flatter tray gives the water longer to soak in before it reaches the lower edge, so less should reach the bottle — the same direction the calculation gives. On any "what if the experiment were changed" question, fix the direction of the change first; it often eliminates every wrong option on its own.

distractorRationale.c: $1180$ mL is $60$ mL *above* the $10^{\circ}$ value. It comes from applying the per-degree change in the wrong direction — adding $5^{\circ}$ worth of runoff instead of subtracting it.
distractorRationale.b: $1300$ mL is the average of the $10^{\circ}$ and $20^{\circ}$ bare-soil values, $(1120 + 1480)/2$. It comes from treating $5^{\circ}$ as though it lay *between* the two tested slopes rather than below both of them.
distractorRationale.a: $1520$ mL is above even the $20^{\circ}$ value of $1480$ mL. It comes from reversing the relationship altogether — assuming that a gentler slope produces more runoff, which contradicts every row of Table 5.

accessibilityText: The question uses the bare-soil row of Table 5: runoff 1120 millilitres at a 10 degree slope and 1480 millilitres at a 20 degree slope. For every other cover the runoff is also larger at 20 degrees than at 10 degrees: gravel 780 then 1010, cut grass 410 then 640, leaf mulch 300 then 505. It asks what the bare-soil runoff would be at a 5 degree slope. The four choices are 940, 1180, 1300 and 1520 millilitres.

provenance.notes: Original item written for this bank against an original experiment description and an invented data set. Not derived from, and not a paraphrase of, any ACT-published question.

independentSolve.workingNotes: Bare soil goes from 1120 mL at 10 degrees to 1480 mL at 20 degrees, which is 36 mL per degree. Extrapolating linearly down to 5 degrees gives 1120 - 5(36) = 940 mL. The 1180, 1300 and 1520 choices are all above the 10-degree value, but runoff increases with slope, so a gentler slope should give less than 1120.

review.notes: Author solved the item and then tried to defend each distractor. Uniqueness rests on direction, not on the precise extrapolation: runoff rises with slope for all four covers, so a 5 degree result must be below the 10 degree value of 1120 mL, and only 940 mL satisfies that. Distractors were deliberately placed above 1120 so that no second option can be defended by choosing a different extrapolation rule. Awaiting an independent blind solve before publication. Option-letter references in the explanation were rewritten to name choice content; the key was re-derived independently and is unchanged. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
